newsitem.title: USA: Strike outcome strengthens Teamsters' Carey.
newsitem.headline: Strike outcome strengthens Teamsters' Carey.

text.p: Teamsters Union President Ron Carey came out in a stronger position after managing the 15-day strike against giant package delivery company United Parcel Service (UPS), analysts said Tuesday.

Carey, who has fought his old employer on and off for about 30 years, was crowing with delight Tuesday after UPS management and the Teamsters reached a tentative agreement which offers the workers significant benefits.
He said the outcome had meaning beyond UPS -- as a milestone toward reviving union activism in a country where union membership is one of the lowest in the industrial world.
"Non-union workers will be talking about how this victory has inspired them to fight for the future, just as UPS workers did," he told a news conference Tuesday.
Alan Draper, professor of government at St. Lawrence University in Canton, New York, said the UPS agreement would bolster Carey's position within the union.
"One of the major criticisms ... in the Teamster election was that Carey hasn't delivered the goods," he said. "This contract is very important in silencing that criticism."

"He (Carey) did face allegations of irregularities in the last union elections so he was keen to show he was effective and had the support of the members. So he did come out well. It is a significant victory," added professor David Jacobs of American University in Washington.

"He is portraying it as a good result for his members. I haven't caught up with all the details but he clearly didn't hurt himself," added Michael Baroody, vice president of the National Association of Manufacturers.
Carey flexed his muscles Tuesday in a new sphere of economic policy, saying major trade legislation would be the next battleground for the union.

He told his news conference the union would fight to stop so-called fast track trade legislation that would allow U.S. officials to negotiate an expansion of the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA) and other trade agreements with limited imput from Congress.
In his earlier union career, Carey had fought great odds to get his job and waged a bitter battle to keep it.
But the 11-day-old strike against UPS by some 185,000 members of the 1.4 million-member International Brotherhood of Teamsters had been his biggest battle yet.
Baroody said Sunday Carey's future would be at stake if the strike ended badly for the workers.

Carey, 61, a long-time dissident and self-styled reformer in a union that for years symbolized labor corruption, was able to capture the Teamsters' highest office in part because the government paved the way for him.
In late 1991 Carey won the presidency in a government-supervised race that was part of a settlement of a 1989 federal racketeering lawsuit against the union.

It was the first time in the union's 93-year history that a Teamster president was chosen by the rank and file instead of convention delegates and it gave Carey, the long-shot outsider in the race, the opportunity he had long sought.
A former Marine, Carey was a driver for UPS for 11 years until he was elected president in 1967 of Teamsters Local 804 in the New York City borough of Queens, where he grew up.

There he represented mostly UPS workers, who once staged a wildcat strike, kept his members covered by a contract that was separate from the nationwide agreement and was always at odds with the union's top brass in Washington.
A darling of union reformers inside and outside of the Teamsters, Carey used the 1991 three-way race to his advantage as his two "old guard" opponents split their vote and left him with a plurality.

Since winning office, Carey has taken a high-profile stand against corruption -- three of his six predecessors went to prison -- and lavish spending. He sold the union's jet, cut his own salary and has put 72 Teamster locals into trusteeships, mostly after evidence of corruption was uncovered.
But he has made many enemies in the union along the way.
A three-week nationwide truck strike he led in 1994 left the union unable to pay strike benefits, and members rejected his proposed dues hike to fortify the treasury.
Late last year, he narrowly defeated James Hoffa, son and namesake of the notorious Teamsters president who was presumed murdered in 1975, in another government-supervised election.

But the bitterly fought election is now under a cloud. A federal grand jury in New York has been investigating the Carey campaign's fund-raising practices, and two campaign aides have been charged with fraud so far.
As a result, the court-appointed officer overseeing the election has not certified Carey as the winner and Hoffa has demanded a new election.
